message.content: {"overview":"Lighthouses went from smoky private fires to a precise international signal network, then lost their keepers and most of their purpose to electricity and satellites.","voice":{"style":"plain, concrete, curious","register":"conversational expert","sentenceRhythm":"short declaratives with the odd long build","narratorPresence":"a guide who points, rarely opines"},"acts":[{"title":"Fire on the Rocks","thesis":"Before optics, a coastal light was a fire that could barely outshine the weather it was meant to beat.","startState":"The listener pictures a lighthouse as a tall tower with a sweeping beam.","endState":"The listener knows that for most of history a light was a smoky fire, private, fragile and short-ranged.","slots":[{"title":"The first lights","beats":[{"claim":"The Pharos of Alexandria stood more than a hundred metres tall and guided ships into the harbour for centuries.","exploration":false,"seed":{"episodeId":"ep-lighthouse-01","startSec":120,"endSec":165}},{"claim":"Ancient lighthouses burned wood or oil in open fires, so their light carried only a few miles.","exploration":false},{"claim":"Roman builders put lighthouses at ports from Dover to the Spanish coast as imperial shipping grew.","exploration":true},{"claim":"The Tower of Hercules in Spain was built by the Romans and still works as a lighthouse today.","exploration":true},{"claim":"Most medieval coasts had no lights at all, and sailors read headlands and church towers instead.","exploration":false}]},{"title":"Coal and candles","beats":[{"claim":"Early modern English lights were often private businesses that charged passing ships a toll.","exploration":true},{"claim":"Coal fires on open platforms smoked badly and could vanish in the very weather that made them necessary.","exploration":false},{"claim":"The first Eddystone lighthouse off Plymouth was swept away in the great storm of 1703 with its builder inside.","exploration":true},{"claim":"John Smeaton rebuilt Eddystone in interlocking granite blocks, a method engineers copied for a century.","exploration":false},{"claim":"Candles and oil lamps inside glazed lanterns replaced open fires because a lantern protected the flame.","exploration":false}]}]},{"title":"The Lens That Changed Everything","thesis":"A French physicist's lens turned the lighthouse from a local fire into a long-range, identifiable signal.","startState":"The listener knows lights were weak and easily lost.","endState":"The listener understands how the Fresnel lens and the flash pattern made every light both visible and nameable.","slots":[{"title":"Fresnel's problem","beats":[{"claim":"Augustin Fresnel designed a lens of concentric glass rings that bent stray light into a single beam.","exploration":false,"seed":{"episodeId":"ep-lighthouse-02","startSec":120,"endSec":165}},{"claim":"A Fresnel lens could send a lighthouse beam more than twenty miles instead of a few.","exploration":false},{"claim":"The ringed lens was lighter and thinner than a solid lens of the same power, which made large lights practical.","exploration":true},{"claim":"French lighthouses adopted the design in the 1820s, and other nations bought lenses made in Paris.","exploration":false},{"claim":"The United States was slow to adopt Fresnel lenses until a lighthouse board reformed the service in 1852.","exploration":true}]},{"title":"A network of lights","beats":[{"claim":"Each lighthouse was given its own pattern of flashes so a navigator could tell one light from another.","exploration":false},{"claim":"Published light lists told captains which flash pattern belonged to which stretch of coast.","exploration":false},{"claim":"Rotating lenses floated on baths of mercury so a heavy apparatus could turn with little friction.","exploration":true},{"claim":"Clockwork driven by falling weights turned the lens, and keepers wound it by hand through the night.","exploration":false},{"claim":"Fog signals such as horns and bells were added because a light was useless when visibility collapsed.","exploration":true}]}]},{"title":"Keepers Leave the Tower","thesis":"Electricity and then satellites took the people out of the lighthouse, and then most of the reason for it.","startState":"The listener understands the lit, staffed network of the nineteenth century.","endState":"The listener sees why the towers survive mostly as landmarks and backups.","slots":[{"title":"Automation","beats":[{"claim":"Electric lamps replaced oil in most lighthouses during the first half of the twentieth century.","exploration":false,"seed":{"episodeId":"ep-lighthouse-03","startSec":120,"endSec":165}},{"claim":"Automatic switches and lamp changers meant a light could run for weeks without anyone climbing the tower.","exploration":false},{"claim":"The United States Coast Guard took over the lighthouse service in 1939 and began cutting keeper posts.","exploration":true},{"claim":"Britain automated its last staffed lighthouse, North Foreland, in 1998.","exploration":false},{"claim":"Keepers' cottages were sold, demolished or turned into museums once nobody needed to live beside the light.","exploration":true}]},{"title":"What the lights are for now","beats":[{"claim":"Satellite positioning lets a ship know its location without seeing any light on shore.","exploration":false},{"claim":"Many coastal authorities have switched off lights that no longer guide any commercial traffic.","exploration":false},{"claim":"Lighthouses that stay lit are often powered by solar panels and small LED lanterns.","exploration":false},{"claim":"Preservation groups keep many towers standing because people value them more as landmarks than as aids.","exploration":true},{"claim":"A lighthouse beam is still the backup a navigator trusts when electronic systems fail.","exploration":true}]}]}]}
